themes.theme: Notifications between authorities about incidents, risks and enforcement measures
themes.definition: Duties on public authorities (and, in one case, on law-enforcement deployers) to tell other authorities about serious incidents, non-compliance, risks, authorisations and testing decisions concerning AI systems.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act builds a chain of 'shall inform' and 'shall notify' duties so that a finding in one Member State reaches the Commission and the other Member States: national competent authorities must notify the Commission of any serious incident 'whether or not they have taken action on it' (#004); a market surveillance authority that finds non-compliance reaching beyond its territory, or adopts measures, must inform the Commission and the other Member States, whose authorities then report their own measures and any objections (#017, #018, #019), and Member States must immediately report findings under Article 82(1) (#021). Authorisations issued under Article 46 must also be reported, excluding sensitive law-enforcement operational data (#087); the establishment of a sandbox goes to the AI Office and Board (#099) and a decision to suspend testing or participation goes to the AI Office (#096); the grounds of a decision on real-world testing go to the other Member States where the system was tested (#010); and the Board, Member States and authorities must give the Commission information on request for evaluations (#028). The Omnibus adds a downward flow, with the AI Office passing serious-incident information 'promptly' to the national market surveillance authority where the provider is situated (#197), and the prohibited-practices guidelines restate the cross-border duty (#135). The only notification held by a public-sector deployer is in those guidelines: each use of remote biometric identification for the Article 5(1)(h) objectives must be notified, after each use, to the market surveillance authority and the national data protection authority (#122 and #127 are the same paragraph extracted by two coders). Content is specified for some notices (identification of the system, origin and supply chain, nature of the risk, national measures, the operator's arguments), and timing words vary ('immediately', 'without undue delay', 'promptly', 'after each use'), but no passage says what happens if a notice is not sent.
themes.holders: National competent authorities; market surveillance authorities (the one acting and those of other Member States); Member States; the Board; the AI Office; and, for remote biometric identification, the deploying law-enforcement authority.
themes.binding: Statutory duties ('shall') in the AI Act and the Omnibus amendments; the guidelines restate them with 'must'. No consequence for failing to notify is stated in any passage.
themes.checks: Not a check in itself. What travels through these channels is the result of an authority's evaluation (non-compliance, risk, a serious incident), not the result of a test of a tool's outputs. Trigger: the finding, measure or incident. Compared against: not stated. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the notifying authority. What happens with the result: recipients report their own measures or objections (#019). For remote biometric identification the trigger is each use, and per the coder note the notices feed the authorities' annual reports to the Commission.

quotes.quote: National competent authorities shall immediately notify the Commission of any serious incident, whether or not they have taken action on it
Where the market surveillance authority considers that the non-compliance is not restricted to its national territory, it shall inform the Commission and the other Member States without undue delay

quotes.location: Art. 1(31)(c), inserting AI Act Art. 75(1a); p. 27
quotes.quote: The AI Office shall promptly transmit the relevant information to the market surveillance authority of the Member State in the territory of which the provider or its legal representative is situated.

Each use of an RBI system pursuing one of the objectives listed in Article 5(1)(h)(i)-(iii) AI Act must be notified to the relevant market surveillance authority and the national data protection authority.

themes.theme: Notification of national rules and frameworks to the Commission
themes.definition: Duties on Member States to send national laws or frameworks made under the AI Act to the Commission or the AI Office.
themes.what_is_set_out: Member States must notify the national rules adopted under Article 5(5) to the Commission 'at the latest 30 days following the adoption thereof' (#066); a recital says national rules 'should be notified' within the same 30 days (#022). The prohibited-practices guidelines restate the duty for national laws on remote biometric identification, add that notification 'does not provide a presumption of conformity' and that the AI Office will confirm receipt (#129, per the coder note), and encourage Member States to send a preliminary draft to the AI Office before adoption (#128), though what the AI Office does with a draft is not stated. The Omnibus moves the moment earlier for a different instrument: each Member State must notify the Commission of any real-world testing framework 'before implementing it' (#194). No passage gives the Commission a power to approve or block a national rule, so the mechanism is informational [inference].
themes.holders: Member States (national or regional legislators); the Commission and the AI Office as recipients.
themes.binding: Statutory 'shall' (#066, #129, #194); recital 'should' (#022); voluntary pre-adoption exchange (#128). The guidelines treat non-notification within 30 days as missing the legal deadline (#129); no other consequence is stated.

quotes.quote: Member States shall notify those rules to the Commission at the latest 30 days following the adoption thereof.
Member States shall notify their national laws to the Commission at the latest 30 days following the adoption thereof .
Prior to its adoption, Member States are also encouraged to send a preliminary version of the national (or regional) law proposed to the AI Office.

quotes.location: Art. 1(25), inserting AI Act Art. 60a(3); p. 25
quotes.quote: Each Member State shall notify the Commission of any real-world testing framework it adopts before implementing it.

themes.theme: Referrals, alerts and mutual assistance in enforcement between EU and national bodies
themes.definition: Formal routes by which national market surveillance authorities, the AI Office, the Commission and the scientific panel ask one another to act, alert one another, investigate jointly or lend each other assistance.
themes.what_is_set_out: Under the AI Act, market surveillance authorities and the Commission may propose joint activities, including joint investigations, for high-risk systems presenting a serious risk in two or more Member States (#007, recital #061); authorities must cooperate with the AI Office on compliance evaluations of general-purpose AI systems usable for high-risk purposes (#008, #062); an authority that cannot finish an investigation for lack of information about an underlying model may send a reasoned request to the AI Office, 'by which access to that information shall be enforced' (#009); and authorities may ask the Commission to use its powers (#023). The scientific panel may send the AI Office a 'qualified alert' about a general-purpose model (#024, #045, #063), which the GPAI guidelines say can lead the Commission to designate it as a systemic-risk model (#260 and #267 are overlapping extracts of one paragraph), and the Board may receive Member States' opinions on such alerts (#119). The Omnibus makes the relationship two-way: all authorities must 'cooperate actively' with the AI Office and assist it (#198); the AI Office must inform the national authority before an inspection or a decision (#200, #202) and gets national help, including police, if an inspection is obstructed (#209); national authorities may carry out fact-finding on its behalf (#203) and receive what its monitoring finds (#204); and a national authority may ask the AI Office, through its single point of contact, to assess a suspected infringement (#201). One Omnibus passage names a public authority's own AI system as the object of enforcement: when the AI Office's action 'involves access to a public authority's data or AI system', it must be assisted by the national authority (#199). [inference] The Omnibus positions national authorities as the AI Office's local arm, whereas the AI Act mainly routes national questions upward.
themes.holders: Market surveillance authorities; the AI Office; the Commission; the scientific panel of independent experts; the Board; national competent authorities and 'the authorities involved in the application of this Regulation'.
themes.binding: Statutory duties and powers ('shall', 'may') in the AI Act and the Omnibus; recitals use 'should'; the GPAI guidelines restate. The only stated consequence is that access to information requested through the AI Office 'shall be enforced' (#009).
themes.checks: Compliance evaluations of general-purpose AI systems (#008, #062): trigger, 'sufficient reason to consider' them non-compliant; compared against, the Regulation's requirements [inference]; metric or threshold, not stated; who, the market surveillance authority with the AI Office; result, the Board and other authorities are informed. Qualified alerts (#024, #045, #063, #260, #267): trigger, the panel's suspicion that a model 'poses concrete identifiable risk at Union level' or meets the Article 51 conditions; compared against, those conditions (the threshold itself is not in these passages); who, the scientific panel; result, follow-ups 'such as investigations' or designation by the Commission. Joint investigations (#007, #061): trigger, serious risk across two or more Member States; metric and use of results not stated.

quotes.quote: it may submit a reasoned request to the AI Office, by which access to that information shall be enforced

quotes.location: Art. 1(31)(c), inserting AI Act Art. 75(1c); p. 27
quotes.quote: When taking investigatory or enforcement action in the territory of a Member State that involves access to a public authority’s data or AI system, the AI Office shall be assisted by the relevant market surveillance authority.

quotes.location: Art. 1(31)(d), inserting AI Act Art. 75(2a); p. 28
quotes.quote: it may request, through the relevant single point of contact designated in accordance with Article 70(2), the AI Office to assess the matter in order to take the necessary supervisory and enforcement measures
the Commission may designate a general-purpose AI model as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk on its own in itiative (ex officio) or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel

themes.theme: Links between AI regulators and fundamental-rights bodies
themes.definition: Mechanisms connecting AI Act market surveillance authorities with the national public authorities or bodies that supervise or enforce fundamental-rights law (the 'Article 77' bodies).
themes.what_is_set_out: Each Member State had to identify these bodies by 2 November 2024 and publish a list of them (#012). The AI Act gives them a power to make a reasoned request to the market surveillance authority 'to organise testing of the high-risk AI system through technical means' (#013), and requires them to tell that authority of requests they make (#011). In the other direction, the market surveillance authority must inform them of serious incidents of the kind defined in Article 3(49)(c) (#005; [inference, from the coder note] incidents that infringe obligations protecting fundamental rights), 'inform and fully cooperate' with them where fundamental-rights risks are identified (#016), and consult them before a finding under Article 82(1) (#020). The Omnibus turns this into a mutual duty to 'cooperate closely and provide each other with the mutual assistance necessary', including exchanging information (#205), and the prohibited-practices guidelines present themselves as enabling such cooperation, citing the Treaty duty of sincere cooperation (#134). The Article 50 guidelines, by contrast, only mark a boundary, saying market surveillance responsibilities do not affect other supervisors' powers, with no procedure for cooperation or referral (#168). [inference] For a public-sector tool this is the main route in the cell by which a rights body could trigger technical testing, but which bodies qualify depends on each Member State's list.
themes.holders: National public authorities or bodies protecting fundamental rights; market surveillance authorities; Member States (for the list).
themes.binding: Statutory duties and powers in the AI Act and the Omnibus; the two sets of guidelines are non-binding interpretation. No consequence for non-cooperation is stated.
themes.checks: Testing on request (#013): trigger, a reasoned request from the fundamental-rights body (the condition for making one is not stated in the passage); compared against, not stated ([inference] the fundamental-rights obligations the body supervises); metric or threshold, not stated; who, the market surveillance authority organises the testing 'through technical means'; what happens with the result, not stated.

quotes.quote: the public authority or body referred to in paragraph 1 may make a reasoned request to the market surveillance authority, to organise testing of the high-risk AI system through technical means.

quotes.location: Art. 1(34)(c), inserting AI Act Art. 77(1b); p. 33
quotes.quote: Market surveillance authorities and public authorities or bodies referred to in paragraph 1 shall cooperate closely and provide each other with the mutual assistance necessary to fulfil their respective mandates

it enables effective cooperation between the competent authorities responsible for the enforcement of the AI Act and the authorities protecting fundamental rights pursuant to Article 77 AI Act and other provisions of the AI Act.

The responsibilities of the market surveillance authorities under the AI Act do not affect the powers and tasks of other supervisory authorities or fundamental rights authorities under their own legal framework

themes.definition: Mechanisms connecting AI Act authorities with authorities enforcing other EU law (data protection, product safety and sectoral law, the Digital Services Act) so that oversight of the same AI system is consistent.
themes.what_is_set_out: When national competent authorities give guidance on an AI system in areas covered by other Union law, they must consult that law's authorities 'as appropriate' (#002, restated in the Omnibus #196), and Member States must facilitate coordination between AI Act market surveillance authorities and those supervising Annex I harmonisation legislation or other relevant Union law (#006). For sandboxes, Member States must ensure cooperation with authorities running other sandboxes (#091), and data protection authorities must be 'associated with the operation' of a sandbox that processes personal data (#095); the Omnibus extends this to authorities providing or supporting access to data (#192). The Omnibus also requires notifying authorities under the AI Act and under sectoral product legislation to 'cooperate in their assessments' (#188), and in recitals asks the AI Office and national authorities to coordinate enforcement with Digital Services Act authorities (#207) and the Commission and national authorities to ensure that sectoral and national supervision does not create overlaps, explicitly 'in the private and public sectors' (#208). The EDPB opinion draws a line between regimes: an AI Act self-declaration of conformity 'may not constitute a conclusive finding of compliance under the GDPR' but may be taken into account by data protection supervisors (#236), who should take 'utmost account' of the opinion for consistency (#237). Most of the AI Act duties are qualified by 'as appropriate' or 'where relevant'.
themes.holders: National competent and market surveillance authorities; Member States; notifying authorities; data protection authorities; the AI Office; the Commission; data protection supervisory authorities (EU074).
themes.binding: Statutory 'shall', often qualified 'as appropriate'; Omnibus recitals use 'should' and 'it is important that'; the EDPB opinion is non-binding interpretation. No consequence stated.
themes.checks: One passage concerns how a check under one regime counts under another (#236): trigger, a data protection supervisor 'investigating a specific AI model'; compared against, the GDPR; the AI Act declaration of conformity may be considered but is not conclusive; metric, not stated; who, the supervisory authority; what happens with the result, not stated.

quotes.quote: Member States shall facilitate coordination between market surveillance authorities designated under this Regulation and other relevant national authorities or bodies which supervise the application of Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, or in other Union law

quotes.location: Art. 1(29), replacing AI Act Art. 70(8); p. 26
quotes.quote: Whenever national competent authorities intend to provide guidance and advice with regard to an AI system in areas covered by other Union law, the national competent authorities under that Union law shall be consulted, as appropriate.

In order to enable AI innovation in the private and public sectors, it is important that the Commission and Member States’ competent authorities ensure that the supervision, enforcement and monitoring of sectoral and national laws do not create overlaps
such a self -declaration may not constitute a conclusive finding of compliance under the GDPR. It may nonetheless be taken into account by the SAs when investigating a specific AI model.

themes.theme: EU-level coordination bodies: the AI Board, its sub-groups and duties to support the AI Office
themes.definition: The standing EU bodies through which national authorities and the Commission coordinate AI Act implementation, chiefly the European AI Board, together with the comitology committee and general duties to facilitate the AI Office and exchange experience.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Board has one representative per Member State, with the EDPS as observer (#109) and, per the coder note, the AI Office attending without a vote. Its role is advisory: it 'shall advise and assist the Commission and the Member States' (#113, recital #057) and 'may' contribute to coordination among national authorities (#114), issue opinions and recommendations, including on amending the high-risk list in Annex III (#115), develop common criteria and benchmarks (#116), cooperate with other Union bodies (#117), support cooperation among sandboxes (#118) and receive Member States' views on qualified alerts and on national monitoring and enforcement (#119); it must set up standing sub-groups for market surveillance and notifying authorities (#058, #112; recital #056 sets the wider framework). Member States must make their Board representative a single contact point and empower them to promote consistency among their own national authorities (#110, #111), and national authorities must coordinate within the Board, to which the Omnibus adds the EDPS and the AI Office 'as appropriate' (#098, #193). The Omnibus also gives the Board a duty to adopt AI-literacy recommendations with common objectives (#206), the prohibited-practices guidelines ask authorities to harmonise even purely domestic enforcement through the Board (#136), and a JRC report suggests a Board sub-configuration could be a forum for AI literacy across public administrations (#251), a proposal only. Duties on the Commission to 'facilitate the exchange of experience' and 'proactively coordinate' (#001, #101), on Member States to 'facilitate the tasks' of the AI Office (#055, #108), and the committee assisting the Commission (#027) leave the content of facilitation unspecified, as the coder note on #108 observes.
themes.holders: The European Artificial Intelligence Board and its sub-groups; Member States and their Board representatives; national competent authorities; the Commission (assisted by a committee); the AI Office; the EDPS.
themes.binding: Statutory duties to establish the Board and take part in it; the Board's own outputs are advice, opinions and recommendations, not decisions. Recitals use 'should'; the JRC suggestion 'may serve'. No consequence stated.
themes.checks: Indirect only: the Board 'may' contribute to developing benchmarks (#116) and may receive national experience on monitoring and enforcement (#119). No trigger, comparator, metric or use of results is stated.

quotes.quote: The Board shall be composed of one representative per Member State. The European Data Protection Supervisor shall participate as observer.
The Board shall advise and assist the Commission and the Member States in order to facilitate the consistent and effective application of this Regulation.

quotes.location: Art. 1(22)(g), replacing AI Act Art. 57(14); p. 24
quotes.quote: National competent authorities, the European Data Protection Supervisor and the AI Office, shall, as appropriate and within their respective competences, coordinate their activities and cooperate within the framework of the Board.

The AI Board, and particularly the sub-configuration on the AI Innovation Ecosystem, may serve as a forum for exchange of good practices and coordination of efforts to advance AI literacy across EU public administrations.

themes.definition: Rules that limit how information passed between authorities, or held in shared registers, may be disclosed.
themes.what_is_set_out: A recital sets a general condition that 'all parties involved in the application of this Regulation' must respect the confidentiality of what they obtain, to keep cooperation between EU and national authorities trustful and to protect intellectual property and trade secrets among other interests (#064). For high-risk systems used by law-enforcement, border-control, immigration or asylum authorities, information exchanged in confidence between authorities may not be disclosed without first consulting the originating authority 'and the deployer' (#014), which gives a public-sector deployer a say over onward disclosure. The Commission and Member States may share confidential information with third-country regulators only where agreements guarantee adequate confidentiality (#015). The prohibited-practices guidelines add that law-enforcement remote biometric identification systems are registered in a 'secure non-public section' of the EU database with limited information and access (#126), and the AI Act keeps sensitive law-enforcement operational data out of notifications of authorisations (#087, under the notifications theme). [inference] The result is that the public-sector uses with the strongest rights implications are the least visible in shared registers.
themes.holders: All parties applying the Regulation; national competent authorities; the Commission; Member States; law-enforcement and similar deployers (as parties to be consulted).
themes.binding: Statutory (Article 78) and recital; the guidelines restate. No consequence stated.

quotes.quote: information exchanged on a confidential basis between the national competent authorities or between national competent authorities and the Commission shall not be disclosed without prior consultation of the originating national competent authority and the deployer
all parties involved in the application of this Regulation should respect the confidentiality of information and data obtained in carrying out their tasks
RBI systems used for the purpose of law enforcement will be registered in a se cure non -public section of the database, with limited information and limited access to that information.

The Commission and Member States may exchange, where necessary and in accordance with relevant provisions of international and trade agreements, confidential information with regulatory authorities of third countries

themes.theme: Coordination of notifying authorities and notified bodies
themes.definition: The machinery connecting the national authorities that designate conformity assessment bodies, the bodies themselves and the Commission, so that third-party assessment of high-risk AI is consistent across Member States.
themes.what_is_set_out: Notifying authorities must develop their procedures in cooperation across all Member States (#075) and notify the Commission and other Member States of each conformity assessment body, and of later changes, through the Commission's electronic notification tool (#076, #079; recital #047). The Omnibus has these notifications, and bodies' applications, use the Annex XIV list of codes and types of AI system, which per the coder note includes generative and general-purpose-AI-based systems and 'Agentic AI' (#189, #210), and requires notifying authorities under the AI Act and under sectoral product legislation to cooperate in their assessments (#188). The Commission must publish the list of notified bodies (#078), ensure that a sectoral group of notified bodies operates (#081) and provide for exchange of knowledge between notifying authorities (#082), and notified bodies must take part (#077). Each notified body must give peers assessing the same types of system information on negative, and on request positive, assessment results (#086), and must warn its notifying authority and clients at least a year before a planned cessation (#080). The Omnibus also obliges notified bodies to accept the simplified technical-documentation form that SMEs and small mid-caps may use (#185). [inference] These passages govern assessment of high-risk systems that public bodies may buy, but none of them mentions public-sector deployers.
themes.holders: Notifying authorities; notified bodies and conformity assessment bodies; the Commission.
themes.binding: Statutory 'shall' throughout; for notified bodies the coder note points to fines under Art. 99(4)(f) (#077). Otherwise no consequence stated.
themes.checks: Sharing of conformity assessment results (#086): trigger, a negative result (positive results on request) and, per the note, refusals, suspensions or withdrawals of certificates; compared against, the Regulation's requirements [inference]; metric, not stated; who, notified bodies; what happens, peers assessing the same types of AI system are informed. The assessments themselves are not described in this cell.

quotes.quote: Each notified body shall provide the other notified bodies carrying out similar conformity assessment activities covering the same types of AI systems with relevant information on issues relating to negative and, on request, positive conformity assessment results.

Notifying authorities shall notify the Commission and the other Member States, using the electronic notification tool developed and managed by the Commission, of each conformity assessment body referred to in paragraph 1.

quotes.location: Art. 1(16), replacing AI Act Art. 30(2); p. 21; A…
quotes.quote: Notifying authorities shall notify the Commission and the other Member States, based on the list of codes, categories, and corresponding types of AI systems referred to in Annex XIV

quotes.location: Art. 1(10), replacing AI Act Art. 11(1) second su…
quotes.quote: Notified bodies shall accept the form for the purposes of the conformity assessment.

themes.theme: Regulatory sandboxes and real-world testing: agreed plans and cooperating authorities
themes.definition: The agreements and inter-authority arrangements governing the testing of AI systems in regulatory sandboxes and in real-world conditions before they are placed on the market.
themes.what_is_set_out: Taking part in a sandbox rests on 'a specific sandbox plan agreed between the providers or prospective providers and the competent authority' (#092); the Omnibus adds 'ensuring that appropriate safeguards are in place' and folds in the real-world testing plan (#191). Testing in real-world conditions requires the provider and the deployer to conclude an agreement specifying roles and responsibilities, without which testing may not go ahead (#106; the recital adds 'effective oversight by competent personnel', #053), and providers may apply to sandboxes jointly with deployers (#102), so [inference] a public body could enter alongside its supplier. Sandbox outcomes feed later checks: exit reports and written proof 'shall be taken positively into account' by market surveillance authorities and notified bodies (#093), and the Commission and Board may see exit reports with the provider's agreement (#094). Around the sandbox sit duties on authorities to associate data protection authorities (#095, #192), cooperate across borders and within the Board (#097, #098, #105, #193), report new sandboxes to the AI Office and Board and suspensions to the AI Office (#099, #096), publish a list (#100, AI Office), recognise participation 'mutually and uniformly' across the Union, including sandboxes run by the EDPS (#104), and involve other actors such as notified bodies and standardisation organisations (#051, #103, #118). The Omnibus adds an AI Office sandbox run 'in close cooperation' with other competent authorities (#190) and requires Member States with real-world testing frameworks to have their authorities 'remove any practical obstacles, including on procedural rules providing access to physical public infrastructure' (#195); a recital asks sandbox participants to follow authorities' guidance 'in good faith' (#052).
themes.holders: Providers and prospective providers; deployers and prospective deployers; national competent authorities; market surveillance authorities; notified bodies; the AI Office, the Commission and the Board; data protection authorities and the EDPS; Member States.
themes.binding: Statutory duties; the agreement in #106 is a condition of testing ('testing may not be conducted' without it). Recitals use 'should'. No other consequence stated.
themes.checks: Sandboxes and real-world testing are themselves checks before market placement. Trigger: development or pre-market testing [inference from the coder note on #095]. Compared against: the agreed sandbox or testing plan. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the provider (with the deployer in real-world testing) under the competent authority's supervision, with 'effective oversight by competent personnel' (#053). What happens with the result: an exit report and written proof that market surveillance authorities and notified bodies take 'positively into account', per the note 'with a view to accelerating conformity assessment procedures' (#093); authorities may suspend testing and must report that (#096); the grounds of decisions on real-world testing go to other Member States where the system was tested (#010).

quotes.quote: the provider or prospective provider and the deployer or prospective deployer shall conclude an agreement specifying their roles and responsibilities
the exit reports and the written proof provided by the national competent authority shall be taken positively into account by market surveillance authorities and notified bodies

quotes.location: Art. 1(22)(d), replacing AI Act Art. 57(5); p. 23
quotes.quote: pursuant to a specific sandbox plan agreed between the providers or prospective providers and the competent authorities, ensuring that appropriate safeguards are in place.

quotes.location: Art. 1(25), inserting AI Act Art. 60a(4); p. 25
quotes.quote: cooperate closely with each other in good faith and remove any practical obstacles, including on procedural rules providing access to physical public infrastructure

themes.theme: Consultation and stakeholder input into EU rules, standards and guidance
themes.definition: Mechanisms by which the Commission and AI Office must or may consult Member State experts, the Board, an advisory forum and the public when making delegated acts, standards, common specifications, thresholds and guidelines.
themes.what_is_set_out: Before adopting a delegated act the Commission must consult experts designated by each Member State (#026; consultations 'at expert level', #065). When preparing a standardisation request it must consult the Board and stakeholders including the advisory forum (#083), and when drafting common specifications it must consult the advisory forum (#084); a Member State that thinks a common specification falls short must tell the Commission, which assesses it and 'if appropriate' amends it (#085), and Member States must help SMEs and other stakeholders take part in standard-setting (#107). The advisory forum must be 'a balanced selection of stakeholders, including industry, start-ups, SMEs, civil society and academia', appointed by the Commission, and advises the Board and the Commission (#120, #059); the AI Office 'should engage with the scientific community, industry, civil society and other experts' on thresholds and on benchmarks and indicators for model capability (#044). Each of the three Commission guidelines in this cell closes with the same invitation to providers, deployers, national market surveillance authorities 'through the AI Board', the advisory forum, researchers and civil society to respond to future public consultations (#131, #174, #265). [inference] Public bodies enter these channels as regulators routed through the Board, or within the general category of deployers; no channel is specific to public-sector users.
themes.holders: The Commission and the AI Office; Member States and their designated experts; the Board; the advisory forum; standardisation stakeholders; providers, deployers, researchers and civil society as consultees.
themes.binding: Statutory 'shall consult' for the Commission in the AI Act; recitals 'should'; the guidelines' invitations are encouragement. The advisory forum's and Board's input is advice [inference: the Commission is not bound to follow it].
themes.checks: Only one passage touches measurement: stakeholder engagement is to inform the threshold and, per the note, 'benchmarks and indicators for model capability' (#044). Trigger: setting the threshold. Compared against: not stated. Metric: not stated in the passage. Who: the AI Office. Result: not stated.

quotes.quote: When preparing a standardisation request, the Commission shall consult the Board and relevant stakeholders, including the advisory forum.
The membership of the advisory forum shall represent a balanced selection of stakeholders, including industry, start-ups, SMEs, civil society and academia.

The Commission encourages providers and deployers of AI systems, national market surveillance authorities through the AI Board, the AI Advisory forum, the research community, and civil society organisations to contribute to this process by responding to future calls for public consultation.
To inform this, the AI Office should engage with the scientific community, industry, civil society and other experts.
